content.title: About
content.content: Rotisserie chicken without skin is tender poultry meat roasted to a golden crust. The rotating heat keeps the meat juicy, while the removed skin reduces fat content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken is one of the most widely consumed meats worldwide.
Rotisserie cooking provides even browning and enhances flavor and texture.
Removing the skin lowers saturated fat and overall calorie count.
Chicken meat is rich in protein, B‑vitamins, and minerals such as phosphorus and selenium.
Rotisserie style is traditional in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern cuisines.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Chicken provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Skin‑less preparation reduces saturated fat, making it heart‑friendly.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains niacin, B6 and B12, supporting metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Phosphorus and selenium in chicken support bone health and antioxidant defenses.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The protein load promotes lasting fullness.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals can be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If marinated with salty solutions, monitor overall sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skin‑less rotisserie chicken can be served as a main dish, sliced for salads, sandwiches, or added to pastas. It pairs well with herbs, lemon, and light sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked chicken in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze portions for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C before eating.

chicken-or-turkey-rice-and-vegetables-ex.title: Chicken or Turkey with Rice and Vegetables (no carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy) and Gravy

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of baked or boiled chicken or turkey, steamed rice, and a mix of vegetables (e.g., zucchini, bell pepper, cauliflower) served with a smooth gravy. It is popular in balanced diets because it provides a good ratio of protein, carbohydrates, and vegetable fiber.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken and turkey are complete protein sources containing all essential amino acids.
Rice is a primary source of complex carbs that raise blood glucose slowly.
Excluding carrots, broccoli, and dark‑green leafy vegetables makes the meal easier on sensitive stomachs.
Gravy is often made from broth and a small amount of flour, giving a creamy texture without excess fat.
Traditionally the dish is served hot, allowing the flavors of meat, rice, and vegetables to fully develop.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Poultry meat supplies the body with essential amino acids needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy provision
items.content: Rice provides glucose, sustaining energy levels over a longer period.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Skinless poultry contains little saturated fat, supporting heart health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both poultry and rice are rich in B6 and B12 vitamins, important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The included vegetables add fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken or turkey proteins.

items.title: Sodium control
items.content: Gravy can be high in salt; people with hypertension should limit its use.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Undercooked poultry may harbor harmful bacteria such as Salmonella.

items.title: Gluten in gravy
items.content: If the gravy is thickened with wheat flour, it is unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot: place pieces of chicken or turkey beside a scoop of rice, drizzle with gravy, and garnish with the cooked vegetables. Fresh herbs like parsley or dill can be added for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared meal in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat thoroughly to a rolling boil to eliminate any possible bacteria.

content.title: About
content.content: Crackers (crispbread) are light, crunchy baked products made from flour, water and a small amount of fat. They are commonly served as a snack, accompaniment to soups, salads or cheese. The texture is crisp, the flavor mildly salty, sometimes enhanced with seeds, spices or cheese.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crackers originated in Europe in the 19th century as a way to extend the shelf life of bread.
There are many varieties, from plain salted to sweet versions with honey or spices.
In some countries (e.g., Sweden) crispbread is traditionally served with butter and fish.
Crackers are often used as a base for canapés and tartlets in culinary applications.
Gluten‑free crispbreads are available, made from rice or corn flour.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Most crackers contain only a small amount of fat, making them suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Crackers provide slowly digestible carbs that help maintain steady blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in fiber (when made with whole‑grain flour)
items.content: Whole‑grain crackers support digestion and promote satiety.

items.title: Contain B‑vitamins
items.content: The flour used supplies modest amounts of thiamine, riboflavin and niacin.

items.title: Versatile pairing with nutrient‑dense foods
items.content: Crackers serve as a convenient platform for protein‑rich toppings such as cheese, avocado, fish or nut butter.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some crackers are high in salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Recipes often contain wheat, dairy, eggs or seeds that can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional crackers contain gluten and are not suitable for individuals with celiac disease.

items.title: Loss of crispness when stored improperly
items.content: Exposure to moisture quickly makes crackers soft and less enjoyable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crackers can be enjoyed straight from the pack, spread with cream cheese, hummus, nut butter, or used as a base for canapés. They are also added to soups and salads for extra crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep crackers in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. For long‑term storage, refrigerate to prevent fat oxidation.

content.title: About
content.content: Flounder (family Pleuronectidae) is a marine flatfish found in coastal waters of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. In Russia it is often referred to as “flatfish”. Its flesh is white, delicate, low in fat and has a mild sweetish flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Flounder can change the colour of its skin to match the sea‑bottom.
Both eyes are on one side of the head – an adaptation to a bottom‑dwelling lifestyle.
In Japan the fish is called “hirasuka” and is used in sushi and sashimi.
Flounder can grow up to 1.5 m and over 30 kg, but is usually sold as fillets weighing 200–400 g.
In the United States it is called “flounder”, while in the United Kingdom similar species are often called “sole”.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Flounder provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The flesh contains very little saturated fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: It contains EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Flounder is a good source of B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for nervous system function.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The fish supplies selenium, phosphorus and iodine, minerals needed for metabolism and thyroid function.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to seafood, including flounder.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Like other marine fish, flounder can accumulate mercury and other toxins; moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: Parasites
items.content: Raw or undercooked flounder may contain parasites; ensure thorough cooking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Flounder is most often served as fillet, pan‑fried, baked or poached. It can be breaded, cooked in a lemon‑butter sauce, added to soups and stews, or used raw in sushi when very fresh, sliced thinly.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh flounder in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic film or in an airtight container, for up to 2 days. Frozen fillets should be stored at –18 °C in their original packaging for up to 3 months. Thaw frozen fish in the fridge before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Kiwi is the edible fruit of the Actinidia deliciosa vine, native to China but now cultivated in subtropical and temperate regions worldwide. The fruits are small, oval, and covered with a thin fuzzy skin that can be green or brown. The bright green flesh is juicy, dotted with tiny black seeds, and offers a sweet‑tart flavor and fragrant aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Kiwi is sometimes called the “Chinese gooseberry,” though its taste is closer to a berry than a pear.
It contains 2–3 times more vitamin C than an orange.
A golden variety (Actinidia chinensis) has yellow flesh and a milder, sweeter taste.
Kiwi contains the enzyme actinidin, which helps break down proteins and is used as a meat tenderizer.
In traditional Chinese medicine kiwi has been used to aid digestion.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Kiwi is one of the richest natural sources of vitamin C, supporting immune function and protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in kiwi promotes healthy digestion, helps maintain satiety, and supports a balanced gut microbiome.

items.title: Good source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports proper heart and muscle function.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Besides vitamin C, kiwi supplies vitamin E, carotenoids, and polyphenols that guard cells against free‑radical damage.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in kiwi contribute to retinal health and may reduce the risk of age‑related eye conditions.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to kiwi, ranging from itching and swelling to severe respiratory symptoms.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Kiwi can enhance the effect of certain anticoagulants (e.g., warfarin), so caution is advised for people on these drugs.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The fruit’s high acidity may irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcer disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Kiwi can be eaten fresh by cutting it in half and scooping out the flesh with a spoon or by peeling the skin and slicing. It is added to smoothies, salads, desserts, yogurts, and sauces. For a milder taste, kiwi can be lightly sweetened or briefly marinated in a sugar syrup.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep kiwi at room temperature until ripe (3–5 days). Once ripe, store them in the refrigerator’s fruit drawer, where they stay fresh for up to a week. Avoid storing near other fruits, as kiwi emit ethylene which speeds up ripening.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned pears in syrup are whole or sliced pears packed in a sweet sugar syrup and sealed in glass or metal jars. The product retains the fruit's aroma and soft texture, while the syrup adds a gentle sweetness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pears are often canned in a light syrup with a touch of citric acid to preserve color.
The syrup typically contains water, sugar, and sometimes flavorings such as vanilla or cinnamon.
Properly sealed cans can store for 2‑3 years.
In the United States, canned pears are frequently used in desserts, salads, and baked goods.
Pears belong to the Rosaceae family and are relatives of apples and plums.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Pears provide both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C helps boost immunity and protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium aids normal heart function and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Canned pears contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in pears have antioxidant properties.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The syrup is high in sugar, so people with diabetes should limit consumption.

items.title: Pear allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pears.

items.title: Can integrity
items.content: Damaged or bulging cans may harbor toxins and should be discarded.

items.title: Preservative additives
items.content: Certain cans may contain additives like sorbate, which can cause sensitivity in some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned pears can be enjoyed as a snack, added to yogurt, oatmeal, salads, baked goods, or used in sauces for meat dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 5‑7 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Pie with chocolate cream is a dessert consisting of a tender crust baked to a golden brown and a rich chocolate cream made from cocoa, cream, and sugar. It offers an intense chocolate flavor and a smooth texture, suitable for both festive occasions and everyday enjoyment.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chocolate cream in the pie is often made with dark cocoa, giving it a deeper aroma.
The classic recipe for chocolate‑cream pie originated in Europe in the 19th century.
These pies are frequently garnished with berries, nuts, or a dusting of powdered sugar.
The combination of a crisp crust and creamy filling makes this dessert popular worldwide.

items.title: Antioxidant source
items.content: Cocoa in the chocolate cream is rich in flavonoids, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: The chocolate cream provides a modest amount of magnesium, important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The pie quickly replenishes energy thanks to carbohydrates from the crust and added sugar.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Gluten and dairy allergens
items.content: The crust typically contains wheat flour and the cream dairy ingredients, which may trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Chocolate‑cream pie is fairly calorie‑dense; moderate consumption is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pie at room temperature or slightly warmed. Cut into portions and pair with ice cream, fresh berries, or a cup of coffee.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the pie in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. It can also be frozen for up to 2 months; thaw at room temperature before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Rusty Nail is a classic cocktail made from Scotch whisky (usually bourbon) and Drambuie, a Scottish liqueur flavored with honey, herbs and spices. The drink gets its name from the rusty‑colored hue that appears when the dark whisky is mixed with the golden liqueur.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cocktail was created in the 1930s in the United States and quickly became popular among whisky enthusiasts.
The name “Rusty Nail” refers to the drink’s color, which resembles a rusted nail.
Drambuie, one of the ingredients, was originally formulated in the 18th century as a medicinal tonic before becoming a liqueur.
It is traditionally served in an old‑fashioned glass over ice.
Variations include adding an orange twist or substituting bourbon with Scotch.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Drambuie’s honey and herbal components provide antioxidants that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Moderate consumption may promote relaxation
items.content: Alcohol in moderate amounts can have a calming effect and reduce stress.

items.title: Alcohol content
items.content: Rusty Nail contains a significant amount of alcohol; excessive consumption can lead to intoxication, liver damage, and other health issues.

items.title: Honey allergy
items.content: Drambuie contains honey; individuals allergic to bee products should avoid this cocktail.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Alcohol may amplify the effects of sedatives and anti‑inflammatory drugs.

content.title: How to Drink
content.content: Pour 45 ml Scotch whisky and 15 ml Drambuie into a glass with ice, stir with a bar spoon. Serve in an old‑fashioned glass, optionally garnish with an orange peel.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store alcoholic beverages in a cool, dark place with the bottle tightly sealed to prevent oxidation and loss of flavor.

content.title: About
content.content: Vegan mayonnaise is a plant‑based alternative to traditional mayo, made from vegetable oils, plant‑based milk, vinegar or lemon juice, and thickeners such as mustard or aquafaba. It contains no eggs, dairy, or other animal‑derived ingredients, making it suitable for vegans and people with egg allergies.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegan mayo is widely used in restaurants that need an egg‑free sauce.
It can be homemade in 10–15 minutes with common pantry ingredients.
Aquafaba – the liquid from cooked beans like chickpeas – is often used to achieve a creamy texture.
Some brands add probiotics to vegan mayo to support gut health.
Vegan mayo typically has lower cholesterol than traditional mayonnaise.

items.title: Low cholesterol
items.content: The absence of eggs makes the product virtually free of dietary cholesterol, which is beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Vegetable oils (e.g., sunflower, canola, olive) provide monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids that support heart health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Depending on the recipe, vegan mayo may be fortified with vitamin E, vitamin K, and small amounts of calcium and magnesium.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: When aquafaba is used, it brings probiotic cultures that can aid a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Allergy‑friendly
items.content: Being free from eggs and dairy makes it safe for people with those common food allergies.

items.title: Allergy to plant ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to soy or mustard oil used in certain recipes.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Like regular mayo, vegan versions are calorie‑rich due to oil content, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Commercial brands may contain artificial preservatives, flavorings, or sweeteners that not everyone prefers.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Salt is often added for taste; people monitoring sodium intake should choose low‑salt varieties.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Vegan mayonnaise works as a salad dressing, dip for vegetable sticks, spread for sandwiches, ingredient in vegan rolls and potato dishes, and as a substitute for regular mayo in sauces, dips, and marinades.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep vegan mayo refrigerated in a tightly sealed jar. After opening, it usually stays fresh for 1–2 weeks. Discard if it develops off‑odors, discoloration, or mold.
